key_findings: Over the period 1991–2025 (35 observations), India's average annual GDP Growth was 6.14% (range: -5.78% to 9.69%).
Multiple OLS regression accounts for 28.40% of the variance in GDP Growth (R2 = 0.2840, F = 2.3005, p = 0.0707).
No individual regressors are statistically significant at the strict 5% level in this specification.

Diagnostic Checks: Durbin-Watson statistic (1.74) suggests no strong evidence of first-order autocorrelation, while Breusch-Pagan test (p = 0.1217) yields no statistically significant evidence of heteroskedasticity at α = 0.05.

correlation_interpretation.summary: Pairwise correlation analysis across 35 annual observations reveals linear (Pearson) and monotonic (Spearman) relationships among economic growth determinants in India. Associations with GDP Growth: Inflation: r = -0.1412 (p = 0.4184, Negative Very Weak / None); FDI_Net_Inflows: r = -0.1182 (p = 0.4989, Negative Very Weak / None); Exports: r = 0.1930 (p = 0.2665, Positive Very Weak / None); Gross_Capital_Formation: r = 0.3180 (p = 0.0626, Positive Weak); Unemployment: r = -0.2095 (p = 0.2270, Negative Weak).

pairwise_interpretations.text: The correlation between GDP_Growth and Inflation shows a negative very weak / none linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.1412, p = 0.4184; Spearman rho = -0.1331, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between GDP_Growth and FDI_Net_Inflows shows a negative very weak / none linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.1182, p = 0.4989; Spearman rho = 0.1140, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between GDP_Growth and Exports shows a positive very weak / none linear relationship (Pearson r = 0.1930, p = 0.2665; Spearman rho = 0.2308, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between GDP_Growth and Gross_Capital_Formation shows a positive weak linear relationship (Pearson r = 0.3180, p = 0.0626; Spearman rho = 0.4305, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between GDP_Growth and Unemployment shows a negative weak linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.2095, p = 0.2270; Spearman rho = -0.3751, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between Inflation and FDI_Net_Inflows shows a negative very weak / none linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.0964, p = 0.5819; Spearman rho = -0.0975, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between Inflation and Exports shows a negative weak linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.2212, p = 0.2016; Spearman rho = -0.0401, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between Inflation and Gross_Capital_Formation shows a negative very weak / none linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.0957, p = 0.5844; Spearman rho = -0.0717, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between Inflation and Unemployment shows a positive weak linear relationship (Pearson r = 0.2869, p = 0.0947; Spearman rho = 0.2320, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between FDI_Net_Inflows and Exports shows a positive strong linear relationship (Pearson r = 0.6973, p = 0.0000; Spearman rho = 0.6829, n = 35). This association is statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between FDI_Net_Inflows and Gross_Capital_Formation shows a positive strong linear relationship (Pearson r = 0.6259, p = 0.0001; Spearman rho = 0.6151, n = 35). This association is statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between Exports and Gross_Capital_Formation shows a positive very strong linear relationship (Pearson r = 0.8249, p = 0.0000; Spearman rho = 0.8255, n = 35). This association is statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between Exports and Unemployment shows a negative weak linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.3506, p = 0.0389; Spearman rho = -0.0826, n = 35). This association is statistically significant at the 5% level.

The correlation between Gross_Capital_Formation and Unemployment shows a negative very weak / none linear relationship (Pearson r = -0.1558, p = 0.3713; Spearman rho = -0.1399, n = 35). This association is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

regression_interpretation.model_fit_summary: The OLS multiple linear regression model explains 28.40% of the variance in GDP_Growth (R-squared = 0.2840, Adjusted R-squared = 0.1605). The overall model F-statistic is 2.3005 (p = 0.0707), indicating that the model as a whole is not statistically significant at the 5% level.

predictor_interpretations.interpretation: The estimated intercept is -1.4300 (SE = 5.2188, t = -0.2740, p = 0.7860). When all explanatory variables are zero, baseline GDP_Growth is estimated at -1.43%.

Holding all other variables constant, a 1 unit increase in Inflation is associated with a 0.1124 percentage point decrease in GDP_Growth (coef = -0.1124, SE = 0.1490, t = -0.7546, p = 0.4566, 95% CI [-0.4171, 0.1923]). This predictor is not statistically significant (p >= 0.05).

Holding all other variables constant, a 1 unit increase in FDI_Net_Inflows is associated with a 1.8653 percentage point decrease in GDP_Growth (coef = -1.8653, SE = 1.2866, t = -1.4498, p = 0.1578, 95% CI [-4.4967, 0.7661]). This predictor is not statistically significant (p >= 0.05).

Holding all other variables constant, a 1 unit increase in Exports is associated with a 0.0092 percentage point increase in GDP_Growth (coef = 0.0092, SE = 0.1491, t = 0.0619, p = 0.9510, 95% CI [-0.2957, 0.3142]). This predictor is not statistically significant (p >= 0.05).

Holding all other variables constant, a 1 unit increase in Gross_Capital_Formation is associated with a 0.3365 percentage point increase in GDP_Growth (coef = 0.3365, SE = 0.2169, t = 1.5517, p = 0.1316, 95% CI [-0.1070, 0.7801]). This predictor is not statistically significant (p >= 0.05).

Holding all other variables constant, a 1 unit increase in Unemployment is associated with a 0.0368 percentage point decrease in GDP_Growth (coef = -0.0368, SE = 0.3334, t = -0.1104, p = 0.9129, 95% CI [-0.7188, 0.6452]). This predictor is not statistically significant (p >= 0.05).

diagnostic_interpretation.heteroskedasticity_breusch_pagan: Breusch-Pagan test for heteroskedasticity yields LM stat = 8.6985 (p = 0.1217). There is no statistically significant evidence of heteroskedasticity at α = 0.05.
diagnostic_interpretation.autocorrelation_durbin_watson: Durbin-Watson statistic is 1.7435 (ideal benchmark = 2.0). DW = 1.744; the statistic is reasonably close to 2.0, suggesting no strong evidence of first-order autocorrelation.
diagnostic_interpretation.residual_normality: Shapiro-Wilk test on OLS residuals yields statistic = 0.9006 (p = 0.0041). Test indicates evidence of non-normality in residuals at α = 0.05.

statistical_cautions: Association vs. Causation: Neither Pearson/Spearman correlation coefficients nor Ordinary Least Squares (OLS) regression parameters demonstrate causal mechanisms. Observed relationships indicate statistical association only.

Sample Size & Observational Data: Analysis is based on 35 annual time-series observations (1991–2025) for India. Time-series data can be subject to structural breaks, macro shocks (e.g., global recessions), and non-stationarity.

Model Specification & Omitted Variables: OLS regression results reflect the 5 specified indicators (Inflation, FDI Net Inflows, Exports, Gross Capital Formation, Unemployment). Omitted macroeconomic variables (e.g., fiscal policy, monetary stance, institutional changes) may influence the estimated coefficients.
